definitions.definition: God as Viṭṭhala (Pāṇḍuraṅga), a form of Kṛṣṇa who came for Puṇḍalīka and stands on the brick, hands on hips, waiting for devotees; addressed as mother (māulī, Viṭhāī); for Narahari Sonār one with Śiva; for Jñāneśvar the Self known by itself.

relations.note: Narahari Sonār's vision of Śiva in Viṭṭhala

name: The vārī and its inner meaning

definitions.definition: The walk to Paṇḍharpūr is outwardly a pilgrimage, inwardly the return of the soul to its mother's home; the saints' company on the road and the name sung together are themselves the tīrtha, and all walk as equals.

relations.note: outer pilgrimage read inwardly: the saints and the name as the true tīrtha

definitions.definition: The succession of saints forms one building: Jñāneśvar the foundation, Nāmdev the walls, Eknāth the pillar, Tukārām the pinnacle (Bahiṇābāī); the tradition is a single work of the saints' grace.

name: The Nāth initiation of the Vārkarī saints

definitions.definition: Ādinātha → Matsyendranātha → Gorakṣanātha → Gahinīnātha → Nivṛttinātha → Jñāneśvar: Jñāneśvar's own statement of the line through which he received knowledge, with the charge to relieve beings in the Kali age.
The one reality appears as god and goddess, being and manifestation, whose union is the world; they are never two.

name: The world as the play of consciousness (cidvilāsa)

definitions.definition: The one self-luminous reality sports as the world without change or second; words, ignorance and knowledge all fall away before it, and the realised live a natural devotion. Readers differ on whether this is Śaṅkara's Advaita or a distinct non-dualism that does not posit ignorance as a principle.

relations.note: the play is the union of Śiva and Śakti

name: The refutation of ignorance and of knowledge

definitions.definition: Ignorance cannot exist in the self-luminous; knowledge as its opposite dissolves with it; what remains is neither knower nor known.
Knowledge does not end devotion: the knower's 'fourth' devotion and the natural devotion of the realised continue without a sense of two.
Devotion is the self-luminous gem that remains when the lamp of knowledge may be blown out; knowledge and devotion both end suffering but devotion is the surer.

relations.note: Jñāneśvar's 'fourth devotion' reads the Gītā's jñānī devotee

definitions.definition: No renunciation is required: grinding, gardening, potting, trading and service become worship when joined to the name; the Lord comes to the house.
Worldly life (prapañca) is to be lived with vigilance and effort alongside the highest aim.

relations.note: the Mahānubhāva ideal is renunciation and wandering

definitions.definition: The name ('Viṭṭhala', 'Rāma Kṛṣṇa Hari') is the easy means for all, needing no rule of time, place or caste; sung together in kīrtan it lights the lamp of knowledge.
Rāma's name is greater than both his formless and embodied forms, mediates between them, is the one support in Kali and the ferrying mantra at death in Kāśī.
Kṛṣṇa's name is the first of the four real things; it saves even when uttered unknowingly (Ajāmila) and removes offences when sung constantly.
Do not be lazy with Hari's name; death is ever at hand.
The name is the jewel-wealth that spending does not lessen and thieves cannot steal.
Rāma's name at dawn, in mind and speech, is the beginning of the day's discipline.

relations.note: the name as the dharma of the Kali age

definitions.definition: Before God birth counts for nothing: saints of every caste are equally revered; outward 'crookedness' of birth does not touch inner devotion; knowing the Veda's meaning belongs to the devotee, not to birth. The saints also record the exclusion they suffered.
Rāmānanda's disciples include a weaver, a cobbler, a barber, a Jāṭ farmer and women (Bhaktamāl); Tulsī scorns caste-talk for himself as Rāma's slave.
Refuge is given to every caste and people, including tribes and Muslims; in the name there is no caste.
Caste does not count among seekers of Parameśvara; women and all castes may renounce.
For high and low the Lord is one (Annamācārya).

relations.note: parallel critiques of birth-rank from within devotion; grounds and institutions differ
parallel critique; the Siddhars argue from the body and yoga, the bhakti saints from devotion
the saints deny that birth decides access to God; not all of them reject varṇa as a social order

name: The marks of the saint (the true devotee)

definitions.definition: The saint calls the afflicted his own, is softer than wax yet firm as diamond, bears insult like water quenching fire, and sees the Lord in all beings.
Rāma dwells in hearts free of lust, anger, pride and greed, that see others' wives as mothers and others' wealth as poison and rejoice in others' good.
The true Vaiṣṇava knows others' pain, helps without pride and speaks ill of none (Narsinh Mehta).
The best devotee sees the Lord in all and all in the Lord.

relations.note: the regional saints' lists restate the Bhāgavata's marks of the devotee
the Gītā's steady-minded one and the saint share equanimity and freedom from passion

definitions.definition: Marathi can carry the highest teaching — Jñāneśvar's words will outdo nectar; if God made Sanskrit, the vernacular was not born of thieves (Eknāth); words are the saints' wealth and weapons (Tukārām).
Tulsī tells Rāma's story in the vernacular (bhāṣā) for his inner joy, in accord with all scripture.
Cakradhar taught in Marathi and bade his disciples keep to it; the scriptures are in Marathi.
Scripture is sung and staged in Assamese and Brajabuli so that all may hear.
Jñāneśvar, alive, entered the chamber at Āḷandī, sat in meditation and was sealed in; he is held to be present there still.

relations.note: the Tamil Siddhars' living samādhi is described in the same terms

definitions.definition: Jñāneśvar's living samādhi, Muktābāī's vanishing in lightning, Tukārām's bodily ascent to Vaikuṇṭha, and Tukārām's farewell 'we go to our own village'.
Mīrā merged into Kṛṣṇa's image at Dvārakā.
Cakradhar, beheaded yet living by his followers' account, departed to the north.
Cāṅgadev's power over beasts was humbled by the siblings' moving wall; powers breed pride, and the yogī of powers became a disciple.
The enticing powers (ṛddhi-siddhi) come to blow out the lamp of knowledge; devotion's gem is untouched by them.
A guru who displays powers or deals in magic is not a true guru.

relations.note: warnings that powers obstruct the goal

definitions.definition: Tukārām received the mantra from Bābājī Caitanya in a dream; Bahiṇābāī and Niḷobā received Tukārām's initiation in dreams; the dream-guru is fully a guru.
Hita Harivaṃśa received his mantra from Rādhā herself, not from a human guru.

name: The marks of the true guru

definitions.definition: The true guru gives knowledge of the Self and removes doubt, is established in the Self and pure in conduct; givers of mantras for gain, showers of powers and dealers in magic are false gurus.
Without a guru even Viṭṭhala's companion Nāmdev was 'unbaked'; the guru (Nivṛtti, Visobā, Janārdana) shows God everywhere; the saint is mother (māulī).
The guru's foot-dust cleans the mirror of the mind; the true guru is the helmsman of the human boat.
The Dāsbodh sets out the marks of the true guru and disciple.
The guru is one of the four real things, with the name, God and the devotees.
Dwelling in the Lord's world, nearness and likeness of form perish with the worlds; union alone lasts.
A moment at God's door with the name wins all four.
Jñāneśvar calls the knower's devotion the 'fourth' devotion, beyond those of the afflicted, the seeker and the one who wants gain.
The coiled power at the base, waked by posture and the locks, rising through the centres to merge in the supreme at the crown (Jñāneśvarī 6; summary only).
Narahari Sonār found Śiva in Viṭṭhala.
Śiva is embodied in sound; the seven notes arise from his five faces; music joined to devotion is worship (Tyāgarāja).
Rāma with Sītā is the supreme Brahman, formless and embodied; the world is full of Sītā and Rāma and the Lord is the master in the form of all beings.

No difference between the formless and the embodied; the formless becomes embodied by the devotee's love; the name mediates between them; yet for the devotee the embodied Rāma and devotion are to be preferred (Bhuśuṇḍi against Lomaśa).
Viṭṭhala standing on the brick is the self-known One; Jñāneśvar's non-dual teaching and the saints' love of the form are held together.
Under Rāma no one suffered bodily, divine or elemental affliction; all loved one another and kept their dharma.
Rāma is the maryādā-puruṣottama; his reign is the pattern of dharma; doing good to others is the highest dharma.

name: The diseases of the mind (mānas rog)

definitions.definition: Delusion is the root of all mental disease; lust, greed and anger are wind, phlegm and bile; cured by Rāma's grace with the true guru as physician, faith, restraint and devotion.

name: The lamp of knowledge and the gem of devotion

definitions.definition: Knowledge is a lamp prepared with great labour and easily blown out by māyā and the powers; devotion is a self-luminous gem needing neither oil nor wick; both end suffering, but the path of knowledge is a sword's edge and devotion melts the Lord at once.
'I and mine, you and yours' is māyā; the world is a colourless painting on the void, neither simply true nor false; worship of Hari alone is real, the world a dream.

name: The dharma of the Kali age

definitions.definition: In Kali neither ritual, devotion nor discernment stands; the name alone supports; yet no age equals Kali for one with faith, since singing Rāma's qualities crosses existence without effort.
In Kali the name sung together suffices without sacrifice or austerity.
In Kali rites, pilgrimages and other gods do not save; Kṛṣṇa's name is the refuge.
Whenever dharma declines the compassionate Lord takes bodies to relieve the good.
Parameśvara incarnates as the five Kṛṣṇas; the incarnations, not the devatās, are to be worshipped.
Nārāyaṇa is the cause of all the avatāras, whom the Kīrtana-ghoṣā praises.
Śiva frees those dying at Kāśī by the power of Rāma's name.
'I am the servant; the Lord is the master in the form of all' — Hanumān's and Bharata's devotion.
Servant-devotion alone is cultivated; the erotic mood is not.
'Keep me as your servant' — Mīrā's plea alongside her bridal love.
Tyāgarāja prefers service near Rāma to wealth; Bhadrācala Rāmadās, Rāma's servant, reproaches his master.

relations.note: dāsya is one of the devotional relationships

name: Devotee, devotion, Lord and guru are one

definitions.definition: Devotee, devotion, the Lord and the guru — four names, one body (Bhaktamāl's opening).

relations.note: the Bhaktamāl's four-in-one and the Ekaśaraṇa's four real things both place devotee, Lord and guru together with devotion or the name

definitions.definition: Love (hita) is the first principle: the divine pair are its two forms, and it is also the path and the goal; Hita Harivaṃśa embodies it.
Rādhā is the supreme object of worship; Kṛṣṇa is her beloved and devotee, fulfilled even by the breeze of her garment; her grace is the only gate.

relations.note: Gauḍīya theology makes Rādhā Kṛṣṇa's bliss-power; the Rādhāvallabhīs make her the supreme object of worship with Kṛṣṇa as her devotee

definitions.definition: The pair's love-play in the groves is eternal, without beginning, separation or departure; separation is only felt within union.
The natural pair play for ever in the nikuñja.

relations.note: the Rādhāvallabha eternal play admits no real separation

definitions.definition: The sakhī's joy is only in the pair's joy; she seeks nothing for herself.
The devotee serves as Rādhā's companion or maidservant, witnessing the pair and delighting in their joy.
The singer is a sakhī in the grove; Svāmī Haridās is Lalitā.
The Rāma-rasik is a companion of Sītā in the inner Ayodhyā.

relations.note: the Gauḍīya maidservant stance is a close parallel

name: The play in the inner grove

definitions.definition: The natural pair (sahaja jorī) Kuñjabihārī and Śyāmā, never joined and never parted, play eternally in the grove; this is the whole of reality for the devotee.
The groves of Vṛndāvana as the eternal scene of the pair's love.
Singing the pair's play in dhrupad is worship; the image of Bāṅke Bihārī appeared in answer to Svāmī Haridās's song.
Music without devotion does not lead to the good path; joined to devotion it is worship of Śiva as sound and of Rāma (Tyāgarāja).
Bargīts in classical rāgas and the sung drama are forms of worship.
Giridhar Gopāl is Mīrā's only husband; for him she casts off family honour and public shame.
The madness and wound of love that only the Lord as physician can heal.
Rādhā's laments in the rains and at the flute's call (Vidyāpati, Caṇḍīdās).
Not real in the eternal union; felt only within it.
Parameśvara's five incarnations — Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Dattātreya, Cāṅgadeva Rāüḷ, Govindaprabhu, Cakradhar — through whom alone liberation is given; grace passes from one to the next.
Souls, deities, world and Parameśvara are eternal and distinct; only Parameśvara liberates.
The gods can give only worldly fruit and are themselves bound; their worship is forbidden to the seeker.
Monks and nuns wander, beg, keep no possessions, harm no creature and dwell in remembrance of the incarnations; open to women and all castes.

name: Sacred places and relics of the incarnations

definitions.definition: Places the incarnations visited and objects they touched carry their presence and are venerated.
The scriptures were copied in special secret scripts and kept from outsiders for centuries.
Liberation is given by Parameśvara alone through the incarnations; the devatās cannot give it.
The devotee does not desire liberation, only devotion.
Liberation is not asked for; remembrance and the saints' company are.
Union (sāyujya) is the only lasting liberation; the accomplished is free while living.
Refuge in Kṛṣṇa alone, excluding other gods, images and Vedic rites; as watering the root nourishes the whole tree, worship of Kṛṣṇa satisfies all.

relations.note: both are refuge in the Lord alone; Ekaśaraṇa adds the exclusion of other deities and centres on the name

definitions.definition: The name, God, the guru and the devotees are the four real things of the dharma.

name: The book in place of the image

definitions.definition: In the nāmghar and sattra the sacred book (Bhāgavata or Kīrtana-ghoṣā) is enthroned on the guru-āsana and worshipped instead of an image.
Monasteries under a sattrādhikār with celibate and married devotees and attached lay disciples, grouped after Mādhavadeva into four saṃhatis; each village has its nāmghar.
The devotees to be honoured are those who do not desire even liberation; one asks only for devotion.
Tukārām asks for no liberation or wealth, only never to forget God and the saints' company.
Beside the pair's rasa, Vaikuṇṭha and liberation are nothing.

relations.note: the four liberations are not sought

definitions.definition: Śaṅkaradeva's account of creation and the cosmic cycle, following the Bhāgavata: from the Lord the principles and Brahmā arise, and the worlds unfold and dissolve in cycles.

name: The four conditions (baddha, mumukṣu, sādhaka, siddha)

definitions.definition: Bound, seeker, practitioner and accomplished: the Dāsbodh's account of the stages of a life.
Effort (prayatna) brings success in both worlds; laziness loses both; effort is joined to devotion to Rāma.
The seeker addresses and trains the mind: go by devotion, remember Rāma at dawn, inquire who is truly happy.
'O my mind, cling to Rāma's feet' (Śaṅkaradeva's bargīt).
'Tell me truly, O mind' (Tyāgarāja).
The accomplished (siddha) abides in the Self, free of doubt, while acting rightly in the world.
Worldly happiness is a barley grain, sorrow a mountain; the avadhūta's teachers teach detachment.
No one in the world is wholly happy; inquire and see.
The saints' company and discernment come only by Rāma's grace; he destroys the sins of ten million births the moment a being turns to him.
As Hari keeps me, so I remain; nothing is achieved by one's own effort.
Rāma never abandons one who comes for refuge (Vibhīṣaṇa).
Living as Hari keeps one.
Tulsī's own nine taught to Śabarī (saints' company first, guileless trust last); any one suffices.
The Bhāgavata's nine expounded one by one, culminating in self-offering.
Of the nine, hearing and singing are foremost.

Sattva binds by attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas to action, tamas to delusion; undeviating devotion carries one beyond them (Jñāneśvarī 14); in Eknāth's bhāruḍ tamas is scorpion venom cured by sattva.
The three states and three guṇas are the cotton from which the wick of the fourth state is spun in the lamp of knowledge.
The mind at death follows the habit of a lifetime; remember the Lord always (Jñāneśvarī 8).
The name uttered at death saves even unknowingly (Ajāmila).

name: The field and the knower of the field

definitions.definition: The body-field of elements, senses, mind and passions is known by the Lord as knower of every field (Jñāneśvarī 13).
